newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: East Europeans welcome agreement on EU talks.
newsitem.headline: East Europeans welcome agreement on EU talks.

text.p: East European leaders, looking forward to the next stage of integration with the West, on Thursday welcomed a European Commission recommendation the EU start membership talks with six states.

Senior Commission officials in Brussels earlier said the Commission had agreed in principle to recommend the European Union begin accession talks with the Czech Republic, Poland, Hungary, Estonia, Slovenia and Cyprus.

"Fine," was Estonian Prime Minister Mart Siiman's first reaction as he broke into a broad smile and shook hands with other members of the Estonian delegation at the second Central and Eastern European Economic Summit in Salzburg.
"We are extremely happy about this and our expectations are getting into reality," Siiman told Reuters, speaking through an interpreter.

"At the same time, we know we are not in the European Union, we have just got a very good acknowledgement and we know we have to do everything possible to go through the negotiations and get into the real accession process."

The pace of European integration is hotting up. The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) said at a Madrid summit earlier this week it would invite the Czechs, Poles and Hungarians to become the first post-Communist members of the alliance.
"I'm glad Poland is in," said Polish deputy prime minister Marek Belka of the Commission decision, declining detailed comment.
The European Commission agreement, which is expected to be finalised in Strasbourg next Tuesday, was a consolation for Slovenia, which narrowly missed out on a NATO invitation.
"We are pleased. We expected it, having in mind the high level of economic development in our country," Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek told Reuters.
"It is a good basis to start negotiations," he added.
But the Commission's list represents a second blow to Romania, which, despite powerful support, also failed to make the NATO cut.

"I believe this is a hasty announcement by sources in the European Commission and this does not reflect the point of view of the heads of state and governments of member countries," Romanian President Emil Constantinescu told Reuters.
He said he still hoped Romania would be among the first East European states to join the EU.

"I have had personal discussions with several heads of states and government and they have told me it is not their point of view (that Romania should be excluded), so I do not believe that such a decision will be taken," he said.
Constantinescu urged Brussels to begin membership talks with all the candidates simultaneously. "I do not believe that one can begin from a hierarchy," he said.
Austrian Chancellor Viktor Klima also expressed surprise at the Commission's stance.

"We are not pleased with the announcement that the Commission recommends six states and it doesn't conform with the Austrian position," he said. "This hasn't just surprised Austria but other European states as well."
The five East Europeans on the list are among the most advanced economies in the region.

Leaders at the Salzburg summit have been assessing the impact of the NATO invitation on economic ties in the area and most have been keen to ensure no new division into "haves" and "have nots" be allowed to arise.

"While (NATO membership) may help us...I would not see the resulting differences quite as dramatic as to constitute a new dividing line," Czech Deputy Foreign Minister Karel Kovanda told a news conference.
